idea.Name: Word-Aware Memory Transformer (WAMT)
idea.Title: Word-Aware Memory Transformers: Enhancing Character-Level Language Models with In-Context Word Summarization
idea.Experiment: We propose to augment the standard NanoGPT character-level transformer with a lightweight hierarchical memory module that mimics the human ability to chunk characters into words without explicit tokenization. The key idea is to segment the input stream into variable-length chunks (e.g., using whitespace/punctuation boundaries) and maintain a fixed-size short‑term memory of summarised past chunks. Inside each transformer layer, we add a cross‑attention sub‑layer that allows every position to attend to the memory slots, providing direct access to distant context beyond the local attention window. Concretely, after processing a chunk, we compute a summary vector (e.g., the average of the hidden states of its tokens, optionally projected through a small MLP) and push it into a FIFO memory of size M (e.g., M=128). For each subsequent position, the self‑attention block is modified: outputs from causal self‑attention are concatenated with the result of attending to the memory (using standard key‑value projections from the memory slots, query from the current hidden state), then fed through the residual connection and feed‑forward network. The memory is stored at the layer level, so every layer has its own set of chunk summaries. During training, we reset memory at document boundaries. We compare WAMT against the baseline NanoGPT on multiple character‑level text corpora (e.g., enwik8, text8, tinyShakespeare). Evaluation metrics include character‑level perplexity, BPC, and targeted long‑range dependency tasks such as bracket matching or copying a sequence over a long delay. We also perform qualitative analysis of generation samples to see if WAMT reduces character‑level errors that arise from forgetting distant context (e.g., forgetting the opening bracket type). To implement, we modify model.py’s CausalSelfAttention to accept an optional memory argument, and in the forward pass iterate through chunks, updating the memory after each chunk. The chunking is done on‑the‑fly using a simple rule based on whitespace; during training, chunk boundaries can be varied from the original stream to improve robustness. This is feasible to implement within the given experiment.py framework, as it only requires extending the attention mechanism and adding a memory buffer, without changing the overall training loop.
